````````text
---
name: task-group-completeness
description: Perform a deep engineering completeness review of proposed task groups against the full stack, complete specs, data model, runtime state, and operator constraints. Repair the injected input card when fundamental tasks are missing, then write the injected report card. Use after task-dependency and before implementation-orchestrator launches workers.
---

## A. Purpose

1. This skill performs a **deep engineering completeness review** of **proposed task groups** before **implementation worker dispatch**.
2. It judges whether the plan is **logically solid**, **technically complete**, and grounded in the **full stack**, **complete specs**, **data model**, **runtime state**, and **operator constraints**.
3. It returns `ready` only when no **fundamental implementation tasks** are missing, and `blocked` when **planning logic** has unresolved gaps.

---

## B. Deep Planning Audit

1. Reconstruct the **implementation logic** from the injected source material, not just the **task list**.
2. Judge whether the grouped plan would produce a **coherent implementation** across **architecture**, **data**, **state**, **APIs**, **UI**, **config**, **migrations**, **tests**, **fixtures**, and **handoff**.
3. Look for **fundamental missing tasks** that would make implementation fail even when every requirement appears mapped and every task appears grouped.
4. Treat traceability checks as **supporting evidence**, not the **audit result**.
5. Reject a plan that is only **performatively complete**: named tasks, mapped requirements, and grouped work are not enough to prove **engineering completeness**.

---

## C. Input Card Changes

1. Repair the injected **input card** before writing the **report card** when deep analysis finds a **fundamental task gap**.
2. Add missing tasks needed for **architecture boundaries**, **data model changes**, **state transitions**, **API contracts**, **UI behavior**, **config changes**, **migrations**, **fixtures**, **test strategy**, and **handoff data**.
3. Amend **existing groups** when they hide **dependencies**, **sequencing risks**, **shared-file collisions**, **missing integration work**, **missing verification strategy**, and **unclear implementation ownership**.
4. Leave a **blocking question** only when the full stack and spec evidence does not determine the **necessary task**.
5. Keep the edited card in the **same structure and style** as this skill.

---

## D. Report Card

1. Write the **audit report** into the injected **report card** after the **input card changes** are complete.
2. The report card explains the **engineering reasoning**, the **planning risks tested**, the **input card repairs**, the **remaining gaps**, and the final **dispatch decision**.
3. Include the **report sections** `Engineering Completeness Findings`, `Fundamental Missing Tasks`, `Input Card Edits Applied`, `Dispatch-Ready Groups`, `Blocking Questions`, and `Dispatch Readiness`.
4. Include **group ids**, **task ids**, **source card ids**, **target files**, **missing engineering logic**, **verification strategy**, **migration needs**, **fixture needs**, **config needs**, **unanswered questions**, and final status using `ready` and `blocked`.
5. Keep the report card in the **same structure and style** as this skill.

---

## E. Hard Rules

1. Do not approve a **group** from **checkbox traceability** without testing the **engineering logic** behind the plan.
2. Do not invent **tasks** without **source evidence**.
3. Do not treat **requirement-to-task mapping** and **task-to-group mapping** as proof of **planning completeness**.
4. Do not leave an **input-card correction** only in the **report card**.
5. Use bold only for the **important words that carry the point** inside a sentence; do not turn each **numbered item opening** into a subtitle.
6. Do not implement **product code** and do not run **implementation tests**.
7. Do not change **card status** during this audit.

Use after `task-list` returns `READY_FOR_TASK_DEPENDENCY` and before implementation grouping is audited.\n---\n\n# Task Dependency\n\n## A. Scope\n\n1. **Purpose.** Convert the flat `task-list` inventory into a dependency graph and implementation groups that can be worked independently where the evidence supports it.\n2. **Start point.** Use this skill only after the upstream `task-list` output includes `Task Inventory`, `Open Questions`, and `Readiness`.\n3. **Readiness gate.** Continue only when the upstream readiness value is `READY_FOR_TASK_DEPENDENCY`.\n4. **Stop point.** Do not implement tasks, run tests, judge group completeness, or dispatch implementation workers.\n\n---\n\n## B. Required Inputs\n\n1. **Task inventory.** Read the complete `task-list` output, including every `id`, `type`, `title`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `action`, `done_when`, and `depends_on` value.\n2. **Source material.** Read any source cards, specs, architecture notes, codebase surface maps, data model notes, runtime state notes, migration notes, fixture notes, and test strategy included with the run.\n3. **Codebase evidence.** Inspect the codebase only as needed to verify dependency evidence, shared ownership, file-family collisions, runtime-state coupling, migration order, and test fixture order.\n\n---\n\n## C. Dependency Construction\n\n1. **Seed explicit edges.** Treat each populated `depends_on` value from `task-list` as an explicit dependency edge before inferring additional edges.\n2. **Infer required edges.** Add an inferred edge only when file ownership, symbol ownership, data flow, runtime state, migration order, fixture setup, API contract order, or test setup proves that one task must happen before another task.\n3. **Classify every edge.** Use exactly one edge type: `hard-blocker`, `shared-file-risk`, `shared-state-risk`, `test-order-risk`, `migration-order-risk`, or `soft-ordering`.\n4. **Ground every edge.** Record the concrete evidence for each edge from task fields, source material, file paths, symbols, migrations, fixtures, tests, or runtime state.\n5. **Preserve uncertainty.** Put unclear relationships in `Ambiguities` instead of forcing a dependency edge or an implementation group.\n\n---\n\n## D. Group Construction\n\n1. **Place every task.** Put every task in exactly one proposed implementation group unless the task is explicitly blocked by an ambiguity.\n2. **Keep collision-prone work together.** Keep tasks in the same group when splitting them would force multiple workers to edit the same file family, state object, migration chain, fixture, scenario setup, or test harness.\n3. **Separate independent work.** Split tasks into separate groups only when their target files, target symbols, tests, fixtures, runtime state, and data assumptions can be changed independently.\n4. **Respect gates.** Preserve sequential gates between groups when one group creates an API, schema, migration, fixture, state contract, or shared behavior that another group consumes.\n5. **Avoid fake parallelism.** Do not optimize for maximum group count when shared-file conflicts would make parallel work unsafe.\n\n---\n\n## E. Output Contract\n\n1. **`Dependency Graph`.** Produce a table with `from_task`, `to_task`, `edge_type`, `reason`, and `evidence`.\n2. **`Independent Task Groups`.** Produce a table with `group_id`, `task_ids`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `independence_reason`, and `dispatch_notes`.\n3. **`Sequential Gates`.** List group-to-group gates with the required completion condition for each downstream group.\n4. **`Collision Risks`.** List files, symbols, tests, fixtures, migrations, data models, and runtime state that make parallel work unsafe.\n5. **`Ambiguities`.** List only dependency questions that block reliable grouping.\n6. **`Readiness`.** End with exactly one readiness value. Use `READY_FOR_TASK_GROUP_COMPLETENESS` when grouping is reliable. Use `BLOCKED_NEEDS_OPERATOR_ANSWER` when an operator answer is required.\n\n---\n\n## F. Hard Rules\n\n1. **No implementation.** Do not edit product code, tests, fixtures, migrations, config, or docs while using this skill.\n2. **No test runs.** Do not run verification commands while creating the dependency graph.\n3. **No invented tasks.** Do not create implementation tasks; report missing or unsafe work as an ambiguity for the next gate.\n4. **No hidden blockers.** Do not put an ambiguous task into a group just to make every task appear dispatchable.\n5. **No duplicate placement.** Do not place the same task in multiple implementation groups.\n6. **No generic rationale.** Keep output concrete and limited to edges, groups, gates, collision risks, ambiguities, and Use after `task-list` returns `READY_FOR_TASK_DEPENDENCY` and before implementation grouping is audited.\n---\n\n# Task Dependency\n\n## A. Scope\n\n1. **Purpose.** Convert the flat `task-list` inventory into a dependency graph and implementation groups that can be worked independently where the evidence supports it.\n2. **Start point.** Use this skill only after the upstream `task-list` output includes `Task Inventory`, `Open Questions`, and `Readiness`.\n3. **Readiness gate.** Continue only when the upstream readiness value is `READY_FOR_TASK_DEPENDENCY`.\n4. **Stop point.** Do not implement tasks, run tests, judge group completeness, or dispatch implementation workers.\n\n---\n\n## B. Required Inputs\n\n1. **Task inventory.** Read the complete `task-list` output, including every `id`, `type`, `title`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `action`, `done_when`, and `depends_on` value.\n2. **Source material.** Read any source cards, specs, architecture notes, codebase surface maps, data model notes, runtime state notes, migration notes, fixture notes, and test strategy included with the run.\n3. **Codebase evidence.** Inspect the codebase only as needed to verify dependency evidence, shared ownership, file-family collisions, runtime-state coupling, migration order, and test fixture order.\n\n---\n\n## C. Dependency Construction\n\n1. **Seed explicit edges.** Treat each populated `depends_on` value from `task-list` as an explicit dependency edge before inferring additional edges.\n2. **Infer required edges.** Add an inferred edge only when file ownership, symbol ownership, data flow, runtime state, migration order, fixture setup, API contract order, or test setup proves that one task must happen before another task.\n3. **Classify every edge.** Use exactly one edge type: `hard-blocker`, `shared-file-risk`, `shared-state-risk`, `test-order-risk`, `migration-order-risk`, or `soft-ordering`.\n4. **Ground every edge.** Record the concrete evidence for each edge from task fields, source material, file paths, symbols, migrations, fixtures, tests, or runtime state.\n5. **Preserve uncertainty.** Put unclear relationships in `Ambiguities` instead of forcing a dependency edge or an implementation group.\n\n---\n\n## D. Group Construction\n\n1. **Place every task.** Put every task in exactly one proposed implementation group unless the task is explicitly blocked by an ambiguity.\n2. **Keep collision-prone work together.** Keep tasks in the same group when splitting them would force multiple workers to edit the same file family, state object, migration chain, fixture, scenario setup, or test harness.\n3. **Separate independent work.** Split tasks into separate groups only when their target files, target symbols, tests, fixtures, runtime state, and data assumptions can be changed independently.\n4. **Respect gates.** Preserve sequential gates between groups when one group creates an API, schema, migration, fixture, state contract, or shared behavior that another group consumes.\n5. **Avoid fake parallelism.** Do not optimize for maximum group count when shared-file conflicts would make parallel work unsafe.\n\n---\n\n## E. Output Contract\n\n1. **`Dependency Graph`.** Produce a table with `from_task`, `to_task`, `edge_type`, `reason`, and `evidence`.\n2. **`Independent Task Groups`.** Produce a table with `group_id`, `task_ids`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `independence_reason`, and `dispatch_notes`.\n3. **`Sequential Gates`.** List group-to-group gates with the required completion condition for each downstream group.\n4. **`Collision Risks`.** List files, symbols, tests, fixtures, migrations, data models, and runtime state that make parallel work unsafe.\n5. **`Ambiguities`.** List only dependency questions that block reliable grouping.\n6. **`Readiness`.** End with exactly one readiness value. Use `READY_FOR_TASK_GROUP_COMPLETENESS` when grouping is reliable. Use `BLOCKED_NEEDS_OPERATOR_ANSWER` when an operator answer is required.\n\n---\n\n## F. Hard Rules\n\n1. **No implementation.** Do not edit product code, tests, fixtures, migrations, config, or docs while using this skill.\n2. **No test runs.** Do not run verification commands while creating the dependency graph.\n3. **No invented tasks.** Do not create implementation tasks; report missing or unsafe work as an ambiguity for the next gate.\n4. **No hidden blockers.** Do not put an ambiguous task into a group just to make every task appear dispatchable.\n5. **No duplicate placement.** Do not place the same task in multiple implementation groups.\n6. **No generic rationale.** Keep output concrete and limited to edges, groups, gates, collision risks, ambiguities, and readiness.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Use after expected behavior is clear and before dependency grouping, orchestration, implementation, or test attribution needs actionable tasks linked to files, symbols, task type, and completion checks.\n---\n\n# Task List\n\n## A. Scope\n\n1. **Purpose.** Convert clarified planning material into an actionable task inventory that an engineer or implementation agent can execute without rediscovering the problem.\n2. **Start point.** Use this skill only after the operator intent, constraints, and expected behavior are clear enough to split work.\n3. **Stop point.** Do not group dependencies, dispatch workers, implement code, run tests, or perform test attribution.\n\n---\n\n## B. Required Inputs\n\n1. **Run source.** Read the source card path passed to the run.\n2. **No source filtering.** Do not ignore source material because its kind is not named in this skill.\n3. **Codebase grounding.** Inspect the codebase enough to link tasks to real files and symbols.\n\n---\n\n## C. Task Construction\n\n1. **Extract work.** Capture each required behavior change, UI change, data change, test need, fixture, config change, doc change, operation, discovery step, and operator decision.\n2. **Discover targets.** Do the additional codebase discovery needed to name target files and symbols before writing the task list.\n3. **Create tasks.** Make each task an actionable codebase-linked change, not a research placeholder.\n4. **Choose type.** Let the model choose the shortest useful `type`. Common terms include `code`, `test`, `scenario`, `data`, `fixture`, `config`, `docs`, and `ops`, but this list is not exhaustive.\n5. **Define completion.** Give every task a concrete `done_when` check that is visible in code review, test output, rendered UI, data state, config, docs, or an operator answer.\n6. **Check coverage.** Confirm the task list covers the requested work or state the blocking question.\n\n---\n\n## D. Type Nomenclature\n\n1. **`code`.** Source behavior, UI behavior, API behavior, state handling, or internal logic.\n2. **`test`.** Automated verification: unit, integration, end-to-end, regression, or harness work.\n3. **`scenario`.** Human-readable behavior path that must be implemented or verified.\n4. **`data`.** Schema, migration, seed, backfill, persisted shape, or data contract work.\n5. **`fixture`.** Test data, mocks, stubs, snapshots, or repeatable setup data.\n6. **`config`.** Environment, build, package, CI, deploy, flag, or tool configuration.\n7. **`docs`.** Required developer, operator, or user-facing documentation.\n8. **`ops`.** Deploy, monitoring, rollback, manual operation, or release task.\n\n---\n\n## E. Output Contract\n\n1. **`Task Inventory`.** Produce one table with `id`, `type`, `title`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `action`, `done_when`, and `depends_on`.\n2. **`Open Questions`.** List only operator answers that block a reliable codebase-linked task list.\n3. **`Readiness`.** End with `READY_FOR_TASK_DEPENDENCY` or `BLOCKED_NEEDS_OPERATOR_ANSWER`.\n\n---\n\n## F. Hard Rules\n\n1. **No implementation.** Do not edit code.\n2. **No verification run.** Do not run tests.\n3. **No generic tasks.** Do not write tasks like `update backend`, `fix UI`, or `add tests` without a target or discovery action.\n4. **No invented requirements.** Do not add work that is not grounded in source material.\n5. **No fake targets.** If the file, symbol, or surface is unknown after discovery, ask a blocking question instead of guessing.\n6. **No report bloat.** Do not add rationale paragraphs, strategy essays, or duplicate sections.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Required Inputs\n\n1. **Task inventory.** Read the complete `task-list` output, including every `id`, `type`, `title`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `action`, `done_when`, and `depends_on` value.\n2. **Source material.** Read any source cards, specs, architecture notes, codebase surface maps, data model notes, runtime state notes, migration notes, fixture notes, and test strategy included with the run.\n3. **Codebase evidence.** Inspect the codebase only as needed to verify dependency evidence, shared ownership, file-family collisions, runtime-state coupling, migration order, and test fixture order.\n\n---\n\n## C. Dependency Construction\n\n1. **Seed explicit edges.** Treat each populated `depends_on` value from `task-list` as an explicit dependency edge before inferring additional edges.\n2. **Infer required edges.** Add an inferred edge only when file ownership, symbol ownership, data flow, runtime state, migration order, fixture setup, API contract order, or test setup proves that one task must happen before another task.\n3. **Classify every edge.** Use exactly one edge type: `hard-blocker`, `shared-file-risk`, `shared-state-risk`, `test-order-risk`, `migration-order-risk`, or `soft-ordering`.\n4. **Ground every edge.** Record the concrete evidence for each edge from task fields, source material, file paths, symbols, migrations, fixtures, tests, or runtime state.\n5. **Preserve uncertainty.** Put unclear relationships in `Ambiguities` instead of forcing a dependency edge or an implementation group.\n\n---\n\n## D. Group Construction\n\n1. **Place every task.** Put every task in exactly one proposed implementation group unless the task is explicitly blocked by an ambiguity.\n2. **Keep collision-prone work together.** Keep tasks in the same group when splitting them would force multiple workers to edit the same file family, state object, migration chain, fixture, scenario setup, or test harness.\n3. **Separate independent work.** Split tasks into separate groups only when their target files, target symbols, tests, fixtures, runtime state, and data assumptions can be changed independently.\n4. **Respect gates.** Preserve sequential gates between groups when one group creates an API, schema, migration, fixture, state contract, or shared behavior that another group consumes.\n5. **Avoid fake parallelism.** Do not optimize for maximum group count when shared-file conflicts would make parallel work unsafe.\n\n---\n\n## E. Output Contract\n\n1. **`Dependency Graph`.** Produce a table with `from_task`, `to_task`, `edge_type`, `reason`, and `evidence`.\n2. **`Independent Task Groups`.** Produce a table with `group_id`, `task_ids`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `independence_reason`, and `dispatch_notes`.\n3. **`Sequential Gates`.** List group-to-group gates with the required completion condition for each downstream group.\n4. **`Collision Risks`.** List files, symbols, tests, fixtures, migrations, data models, and runtime state that make parallel work unsafe.\n5. **`Ambiguities`.** List only dependency questions that block reliable grouping.\n6. **`Readiness`.** End with exactly one readiness value. Use `READY_FOR_TASK_GROUP_COMPLETENESS` when grouping is reliable. Use `BLOCKED_NEEDS_OPERATOR_ANSWER` when an operator answer is required.\n\n---\n\n## F. Hard Rules\n\n1. **No implementation.** Do not edit product code, tests, fixtures, migrations, config, or docs while using this skill.\n2. **No test runs.** Do not run verification commands while creating the dependency graph.\n3. **No invented tasks.** Do not create implementation tasks; report missing or unsafe work as an ambiguity for the next gate.\n4. **No hidden blockers.** Do not put an ambiguous task into a group just to make every task appear dispatchable.\n5. **No duplicate placement.** Do not place the same task in multiple implementation groups.\n6. **No generic rationale.** Keep output concrete and limited to edges, groups, gates, collision risks, ambiguities, and readiness.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}
.decision-os/threads/bugs/thread-card-codex-skill-1783614296635-41b41034.md:2918:.decision-os/runs/codex-skills/bugs/codex-skill-1783611210436-8e41c0b2.jsonl:5:{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_1","type":"command_execution","command":"/usr/bin/zsh -lc 'cat /home/jbb/.codex/skills/task-list/SKILL.md'","aggregated_output":"---\nname: task-list\ndescription: Create concise, codebase-grounded task inventories from a clarified Decision OS source card and any run-provided source material. Use after expected behavior is clear and before dependency grouping, orchestration, implementation, or test attribution needs actionable tasks linked to files, symbols, task type, and completion checks.\n---\n\n# Task List\n\n## A. Scope\n\n1. **Purpose.** Convert clarified planning material into an actionable task inventory that an engineer or implementation agent can execute without rediscovering the problem.\n2. **Start point.** Use this skill only after the operator intent, constraints, and expected behavior are clear enough to split work.\n3. **Stop point.** Do not group dependencies, dispatch workers, implement code, run tests, or perform test attribution.\n\n---\n\n## B. Required Inputs\n\n1. **Run source.** Read the source card path passed to the run.\n2. **No source filtering.** Do not ignore source material because its kind is not named in this skill.\n3. **Codebase grounding.** Inspect the codebase enough to link tasks to real files and symbols.\n\n---\n\n## C. Task Construction\n\n1. **Extract work.** Capture each required behavior change, UI change, data change, test need, fixture, config change, doc change, operation, discovery step, and operator decision.\n2. **Discover targets.** Do the additional codebase discovery needed to name target files and symbols before writing the task list.\n3. **Create tasks.** Make each task an actionable codebase-linked change, not a research placeholder.\n4. **Choose type.** Let the model choose the shortest useful `type`. Common terms include `code`, `test`, `scenario`, `data`, `fixture`, `config`, `docs`, and `ops`, but this list is not exhaustive.\n5. **Define completion.** Give every task a concrete `done_when` check that is visible in code review, test output, rendered UI, data state, config, docs, or an operator answer.\n6. **Check coverage.** Confirm the task list covers the requested work or state the blocking question.\n\n---\n\n## D. Type Nomenclature\n\n1. **`code`.** Source behavior, UI behavior, API behavior, state handling, or internal logic.\n2. **`test`.** Automated verification: unit, integration, end-to-end, regression, or harness work.\n3. **`scenario`.** Human-readable behavior path that must be implemented or verified.\n4. **`data`.** Schema, migration, seed, backfill, persisted shape, or data contract work.\n5. **`fixture`.** Test data, mocks, stubs, snapshots, or repeatable setup data.\n6. **`config`.** Environment, build, package, CI, deploy, flag, or tool configuration.\n7. **`docs`.** Required developer, operator, or user-facing documentation.\n8. **`ops`.** Deploy, monitoring, rollback, manual operation, or release task.\n\n---\n\n## E. Output Contract\n\n1. **`Task Inventory`.** Produce one table with `id`, `type`, `title`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `action`, `done_when`, and `depends_on`.\n2. **`Open Questions`.** List only operator answers that block a reliable codebase-linked task list.\n3. **`Readiness`.** End with `READY_FOR_TASK_DEPENDENCY` or `BLOCKED_NEEDS_OPERATOR_ANSWER`.\n\n---\n\n## F. Hard Rules\n\n1. **No implementation.** Do not edit code.\n2. **No verification run.** Do not run tests.\n3. **No generic tasks.** Do not write tasks like `update backend`, `fix UI`, or `add tests` without a target or discovery action.\n4. **No invented requirements.** Do not add work that is not grounded in source material.\n5. **No fake targets.** If the file, symbol, or surface is unknown after discovery, ask a blocking question instead of guessing.\n6. **No report bloat.** Do not add rationale paragraphs, strategy essays, or duplicate sections.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

.decision-os/runs/codex-skills/ux/codex-skill-1783658255872-5630c522.jsonl:5:{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_1","type":"command_execution","command":"/usr/bin/zsh -lc \"sed -n '1,240p' /home/jbb/.codex/skills/task-list/SKILL.md && git status --short && rg --files backend/src frontend/src frontend/assets | rg '(read-card-skill-run-controller|render-thread-panel|render-thread-notes|request-card-skill-run-status|poll-card-skill-run|thread\\\\.css|thread|codex)' | sed -n '1,240p'\"","aggregated_output":"---\nname: task-list\ndescription: Create concise, codebase-grounded task inventories from a clarified Decision OS source card and any run-provided source material. Use after expected behavior is clear and before dependency grouping, orchestration, implementation, or test attribution needs actionable tasks linked to files, symbols, task type, and completion checks.\n---\n\n# Task List\n\n## A. Scope\n\n1. **Purpose.** Convert clarified planning material into an actionable task inventory that an engineer or implementation agent can execute without rediscovering the problem.\n2. **Start point.** Use this skill only after the operator intent, constraints, and expected behavior are clear enough to split work.\n3. **Stop point.** Do not group dependencies, dispatch workers, implement code, run tests, or perform test attribution.\n\n---\n\n## B. Required Inputs\n\n1. **Run source.** Read the source card path passed to the run.\n2. **No source filtering.** Do not ignore source material because its kind is not named in this skill.\n3. **Codebase grounding.** Inspect the codebase enough to link tasks to real files and symbols.\n\n---\n\n## C. Task Construction\n\n1. **Extract work.** Capture each required behavior change, UI change, data change, test need, fixture, config change, doc change, operation, discovery step, and operator decision.\n2. **Discover targets.** Do the additional codebase discovery needed to name target files and symbols before writing the task list.\n3. **Create tasks.** Make each task an actionable codebase-linked change, not a research placeholder.\n4. **Choose type.** Let the model choose the shortest useful `type`. Common terms include `code`, `test`, `scenario`, `data`, `fixture`, `config`, `docs`, and `ops`, but this list is not exhaustive.\n5. **Define completion.** Give every task a concrete `done_when` check that is visible in code review, test output, rendered UI, data state, config, docs, or an operator answer.\n6. **Check coverage.** Confirm the task list covers the requested work or state the blocking question.\n\n---\n\n## D. Type Nomenclature\n\n1. **`code`.** Source behavior, UI behavior, API behavior, state handling, or internal logic.\n2. **`test`.** Automated verification: unit, integration, end-to-end, regression, or harness work.\n3. **`scenario`.** Human-readable behavior path that must be implemented or verified.\n4. **`data`.** Schema, migration, seed, backfill, persisted shape, or data contract work.\n5. **`fixture`.** Test data, mocks, stubs, snapshots, or repeatable setup data.\n6. **`config`.** Environment, build, package, CI, deploy, flag, or tool configuration.\n7. **`docs`.** Required developer, operator, or user-facing documentation.\n8. **`ops`.** Deploy, monitoring, rollback, manual operation, or release task.\n\n---\n\n## E. Output Contract\n\n1. **`Task Inventory`.** Produce one table with `id`, `type`, `title`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `action`, `done_when`, and `depends_on`.\n2. **`Open Questions`.** List only operator answers that block a reliable codebase-linked task list.\n3. **`Readiness`.** End with `READY_FOR_TASK_DEPENDENCY` or `BLOCKED_NEEDS_OPERATOR_ANSWER`.\n\n---\n\n## F. Hard Rules\n\n1. **No implementation.** Do not edit code.\n2. **No verification run.** Do not run tests.\n3. **No generic tasks.** Do not write tasks like `update backend`, `fix UI`, or `add tests` without a target or discovery action.\n4. **No invented requirements.** Do not add work that is not grounded in source material.\n5. **No fake targets.** If the file, symbol, or surface is unknown after discovery, ask a blocking question instead of guessing.\n6. **No report bloat.** Do not add rationale paragraphs, strategy essays, or duplicate sections.\n M Scope\n\n1. **Purpose.** Convert clarified planning material into an actionable task inventory that an engineer or implementation agent can execute without rediscovering the problem.\n2. **Start point.** Use this skill only after the operator intent, constraints, and expected behavior are clear enough to split work.\n3. **Stop point.** Do not group dependencies, dispatch workers, implement code, run tests, or perform test attribution.\n\n---\n\n## B. Required Inputs\n\n1. **Run source.** Read the source card path passed to the run.\n2. **No source filtering.** Do not ignore source material because its kind is not named in this skill.\n3. **Codebase grounding.** Inspect the codebase enough to link tasks to real files and symbols.\n\n---\n\n## C. Task Construction\n\n1. **Extract work.** Capture each required behavior change, UI change, data change, test need, fixture, config change, doc change, operation, discovery step, and operator decision.\n2. **Discover targets.** Do the additional codebase discovery needed to name target files and symbols before writing the task list.\n3. **Create tasks.** Make each task an actionable codebase-linked change, not a research placeholder.\n4. **Choose type.** Let the model choose the shortest useful `type`. Common terms include `code`, `test`, `scenario`, `data`, `fixture`, `config`, `docs`, and `ops`, but this list is not exhaustive.\n5. **Define completion.** Give every task a concrete `done_when` check that is visible in code review, test output, rendered UI, data state, config, docs, or an operator answer.\n6. **Check coverage.** Confirm the task list covers the requested work or state the blocking question.\n\n---\n\n## D. Type Nomenclature\n\n1. **`code`.** Source behavior, UI behavior, API behavior, state handling, or internal logic.\n2. **`test`.** Automated verification: unit, integration, end-to-end, regression, or harness work.\n3. **`scenario`.** Human-readable behavior path that must be implemented or verified.\n4. **`data`.** Schema, migration, seed, backfill, persisted shape, or data contract work.\n5. **`fixture`.** Test data, mocks, stubs, snapshots, or repeatable setup data.\n6. **`config`.** Environment, build, package, CI, deploy, flag, or tool configuration.\n7. **`docs`.** Required developer, operator, or user-facing documentation.\n8. **`ops`.** Deploy, monitoring, rollback, manual operation, or release task.\n\n---\n\n## E. Output Contract\n\n1. **`Task Inventory`.** Produce one table with `id`, `type`, `title`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `action`, `done_when`, and `depends_on`.\n2. **`Open Questions`.** List only operator answers that block a reliable codebase-linked task list.\n3. **`Readiness`.** End with `READY_FOR_TASK_DEPENDENCY` or `BLOCKED_NEEDS_OPERATOR_ANSWER`.\n\n---\n\n## F. Hard Rules\n\n1. **No implementation.** Do not edit code.\n2. **No verification run.** Do not run tests.\n3. **No generic tasks.** Do not write tasks like `update backend`, `fix UI`, or `add tests` without a target or discovery action.\n4. **No invented requirements.** Do not add work that is not grounded in source material.\n5. **No fake targets.** If the file, symbol, or surface is unknown after discovery, ask a blocking question instead of guessing.\n6. **No report bloat.** Do not add rationale paragraphs, strategy essays, or duplicate sections.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Use after `task-list` returns `READY_FOR_TASK_DEPENDENCY` and before implementation grouping is audited.\n---\n\n# Task Dependency\n\n## A. Scope\n\n1. **Purpose.** Convert the flat `task-list` inventory into a dependency graph and implementation groups that can be worked independently where the evidence supports it.\n2. **Start point.** Use this skill only after the upstream `task-list` output includes `Task Inventory`, `Open Questions`, and `Readiness`.\n3. **Readiness gate.** Continue only when the upstream readiness value is `READY_FOR_TASK_DEPENDENCY`.\n4. **Stop point.** Do not implement tasks, run tests, judge group completeness, or dispatch implementation workers.\n\n---\n\n## B. Required Inputs\n\n1. **Task inventory.** Read the complete `task-list` output, including every `id`, `type`, `title`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `action`, `done_when`, and `depends_on` value.\n2. **Source material.** Read any source cards, specs, architecture notes, codebase surface maps, data model notes, runtime state notes, migration notes, fixture notes, and test strategy included with the run.\n3. **Codebase evidence.** Inspect the codebase only as needed to verify dependency evidence, shared ownership, file-family collisions, runtime-state coupling, migration order, and test fixture order.\n\n---\n\n## C. Dependency Construction\n\n1. **Seed explicit edges.** Treat each populated `depends_on` value from `task-list` as an explicit dependency edge before inferring additional edges.\n2. **Infer required edges.** Add an inferred edge only when file ownership, symbol ownership, data flow, runtime state, migration order, fixture setup, API contract order, or test setup proves that one task must happen before another task.\n3. **Classify every edge.** Use exactly one edge type: `hard-blocker`, `shared-file-risk`, `shared-state-risk`, `test-order-risk`, `migration-order-risk`, or `soft-ordering`.\n4. **Ground every edge.** Record the concrete evidence for each edge from task fields, source material, file paths, symbols, migrations, fixtures, tests, or runtime state.\n5. **Preserve uncertainty.** Put unclear relationships in `Ambiguities` instead of forcing a dependency edge or an implementation group.\n\n---\n\n## D. Group Construction\n\n1. **Place every task.** Put every task in exactly one proposed implementation group unless the task is explicitly blocked by an ambiguity.\n2. **Keep collision-prone work together.** Keep tasks in the same group when splitting them would force multiple workers to edit the same file family, state object, migration chain, fixture, scenario setup, or test harness.\n3. **Separate independent work.** Split tasks into separate groups only when their target files, target symbols, tests, fixtures, runtime state, and data assumptions can be changed independently.\n4. **Respect gates.** Preserve sequential gates between groups when one group creates an API, schema, migration, fixture, state contract, or shared behavior that another group consumes.\n5. **Avoid fake parallelism.** Do not optimize for maximum group count when shared-file conflicts would make parallel work unsafe.\n\n---\n\n## E. Output Contract\n\n1. **`Dependency Graph`.** Produce a table with `from_task`, `to_task`, `edge_type`, `reason`, and `evidence`.\n2. **`Independent Task Groups`.** Produce a table with `group_id`, `task_ids`, `target_files`, `target_symbols`, `independence_reason`, and `dispatch_notes`.\n3. **`Sequential Gates`.** List group-to-group gates with the required completion condition for each downstream group.\n4. **`Collision Risks`.** List files, symbols, tests, fixtures, migrations, data models, and runtime state that make parallel work unsafe.\n5. **`Ambiguities`.** List only dependency questions that block reliable grouping.\n6. **`Readiness`.** End with exactly one readiness value. Use `READY_FOR_TASK_GROUP_COMPLETENESS` when grouping is reliable. Use `BLOCKED_NEEDS_OPERATOR_ANSWER` when an operator answer is required.\n\n---\n\n## F. Hard Rules\n\n1. **No implementation.** Do not edit product code, tests, fixtures, migrations, config, or docs while using this skill.\n2. **No test runs.** Do not run verification commands while creating the dependency graph.\n3. **No invented tasks.** Do not create implementation tasks; report missing or unsafe work as an ambiguity for the next gate.\n4. **No hidden blockers.** Do not put an ambiguous task into a group just to make every task appear dispatchable.\n5. **No duplicate placement.** Do not place the same task in multiple implementation groups.\n6. **No generic rationale.** Keep output concrete and limited to edges, groups, gates, collision risks, ambiguities, and readiness.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Scope\n554-\n555:1. **Purpose:** Launch implementation workers from approved independent task groups and coordinate the batch until every group has returned a result.\n556-2. **Ownership:** Own dispatch, worker result collection, test attribution handoff, root-cause routing, and repair-loop coordination.\n557:3. **Boundary:** Do not implement code directly unless the orchestrator is explicitly assigned an `implementation-worker` role for one group.\n558-\n559----\n560-\n561-## B. Required Inputs\n562-\n563-1. **Task groups:** Read the approved independent groups from `task-group-completeness`.\n564-2. **Dependency graph:** Read group ordering and blocking edges from `task-dependency`.\n565-3. **Task inventory:** Read source task ids, target paths, acceptance checks, and evidence links from `task-list`.\n566:4. **Worker contract:** Identify the implementation worker skill used for each dispatch.\n567-5. **Test contract:** Identify the `test-failure-attribution` input format that receives the completed batch.\n568-\n569----\n570-\n571-## C. Dispatch Workflow\n572-\n573-1. **Build packages:** Create one dispatch package per ready group with `groupId`, `taskIds`, target paths, acceptance checks, source references, and forbidden out-of-scope areas.\n574:2. **Launch workers:** Start one implementation worker for each independent group using available agent tooling.\n575:3. **Protect global tests:** Do not run global tests while implementation workers are active.\n576-4. **Track status:** Use the exact worker statuses `pending`, `running`, `returned`, `blocked`, and `needs-repair`.\n577-5. **Collect returns:** When every worker has returned, collect changed files, completed task ids, blockers, and assumptions.\n578-6. **Handoff tests:** Send the completed batch to `test-failure-attribution` with the test commands, changed files, completed task ids, and worker notes.\n579-7. **Route failures:** Dispatch fix workers for clear group-owned failures and dispatch `root-cause-analysis` for ambiguous failures.\n--\n599-4. **No requirement inference:** Do not ask a worker to infer missing requirements that should have been handled by `task-group-completeness`.\n600-````\n601-\n602-# AGENT\n603:<!-- implementation-orchestrator\n1677:description: Orchestrate parallel implementation workers from complete independent task groups, collect their results, then coordinate test attribution, RCA, and repair loops. Use after task groups pass task-group-completeness and before any global test run.\n1678----\n1679-\n1680-# Implementation Orchestrator\n1681-\n1682-## A. Scope\n1683-\n1684:1. **Purpose:** Launch implementation workers from approved independent task groups and coordinate the batch until every group has returned a result.\n1685-2. **Ownership:** Own dispatch, worker result collection, test attribution handoff, root-cause routing, and repair-loop coordination.\n1686:3. **Boundary:** Do not implement code directly unless the orchestrator is explicitly assigned an `implementation-worker` role for one group.\n1687-\n1688----\n1689-\n1690-## B. Required Inputs\n1691-\n1692-1. **Task groups:** Read the approved independent groups from `task-group-completeness`.\n1693-2. **Dependency graph:** Read group ordering and blocking edges from `task-dependency`.\n1694-3. **Task inventory:** Read source task ids, target paths, acceptance checks, and evidence links from `task-list`.\n1695:4. **Worker contract:** Identify the implementation worker skill used for each dispatch.\n1696-5. **Test contract:** Identify the `test-failure-attribution` input format that receives the completed batch.\n1697-\n1698----\n1699-\n1700-## C. Dispatch Workflow\n1701-\n1702-1. **Build packages:** Create one dispatch package per ready group with `groupId`, `taskIds`, target paths, acceptance checks, source references, and forbidden out-of-scope areas.\n1703:2. **Launch workers:** Start one implementation worker for each independent group using available agent tooling.\n1704:3. **Protect global tests:** Do not run global tests while implementation workers are active.\n1705-4. **Track status:** Use the exact worker statuses `pending`, `running`, `returned`, `blocked`, and `needs-repair`.\n1706-5. **Collect returns:** When every worker has returned, collect changed files, completed task ids, blockers, and assumptions.\n1707-6. **Handoff tests:** Send the completed batch to `test-failure-attribution` with the test commands, changed files, completed task ids, and worker notes.\n1708-7. **Route failures:** Dispatch fix workers for clear group-owned failures and dispatch `root-cause-analysis` for ambiguous failures.\n--\n1728-4. **No requirement inference:** Do not ask a worker to infer missing requirements that should have been handled by `task-group-completeness`.\n1729-````\n1730-\n1731-# repair loops. Use after task groups pass task-group-completeness and before any global test run.\n2810----\n2811-\n2812-# Implementation Orchestrator\n2813-\n2814-## A. Scope\n2815-\n2816:1. Launch implementation workers from **approved independent task groups** and coordinate the batch until every group has returned a result.\n2817-2. Own `dispatch`, `worker result collection`, `test attribution handoff`, `root-cause routing`, and `repair-loop coordination`.\n2818:3. Do not implement code directly unless the orchestrator is explicitly assigned an `implementation-worker` role for one group.\n2819-\n2820----\n2821-\n2822-## B. Required Inputs\n2823-\n2824-1. Read approved independent groups from `task-group-completeness`.\n2825-2. Read group ordering and blocking edges from `task-dependency`.\n2826-3. Read source `taskIds`, `targetPaths`, `acceptanceChecks`, and evidence links from `task-list`.\n2827:4. Identify the implementation worker skill used for each `dispatch`.\n2828-5. Identify the `test-failure-attribution` input format that receives the completed batch.\n2829-\n2830----\n2831-\n2832-## C. Dispatch Workflow\n2833-\n2834-1. Create one `dispatch package` per ready group with `groupId`, `taskIds`, `targetPaths`, `acceptanceChecks`, `sourceReferences`, and `forbiddenScopes`.\n2835:2. Start **one implementation worker per independent group** using available agent tooling.\n2836:3. Do not run `global tests` while implementation workers are active.\n2837-4. Track worker status with `pending`, `running`, `returned`, `blocked`, and `needs-repair`.\n2838-5. After every worker returns, collect `changedFiles`, `completedTaskIds`, `blockers`, and `assumptions`.\n2839-6. Send the completed batch to `test-failure-attribution` with `testCommands`, `changedFiles`, `completedTaskIds`, and worker notes.\n2840-7. Dispatch fix workers for **clear group-owned failures** and dispatch `root-cause-analysis` for ambiguous failures.\n--\n2860-4. Launch implementation workers from **approved independent task groups** and coordinate the batch until every group has returned a result.\n3319-2. Own `dispatch`, `worker result collection`, `test attribution handoff`, `root-cause routing`, and `repair-loop coordination`.\n3320:3. Do not implement code directly unless the orchestrator is explicitly assigned an `implementation-worker` role for one group.\n3321-\n3322----\n3323-\n3324-## B. Required Inputs\n3325-\n3326-1. Read approved independent groups from `task-group-completeness`.\n3327-2. Read group ordering and blocking edges from `task-dependency`.\n3328-3. Read source `taskIds`, `targetPaths`, `acceptanceChecks`, and evidence links from `task-list`.\n3329:4. Identify the implementation worker skill used for each `dispatch`.\n3330-5. Identify the `test-failure-attribution` input format that receives the completed batch.\n3331-\n3332----\n3333-\n3334-## C. Dispatch Workflow\n3335-\n3336-1. Create one `dispatch package` per ready group with `groupId`, `taskIds`, `targetPaths`, `acceptanceChecks`, `sourceReferences`, and `forbiddenScopes`.\n3337:2. Start **one implementation worker per independent group** using available agent tooling.\n3338:3. Do not run `global tests` while implementation workers are active.\n3339-4. Track `worker status` with `pending`, `running`, `returned`, `blocked`, and `needs-repair`.\n3340-5. After every worker returns, collect `changedFiles`, `completedTaskIds`, `blockers`, and `assumptions`.\n3341-6. Send the completed batch to `test-failure-attribution` with `testCommands`, `changedFiles`, `completedTaskIds`, and worker notes.\n3342-7. Include group id, task ids, target paths, acceptance checks, source references, and forbidden out-of-scope areas.\n4367:2. Track worker status as `pending`, `running`, `returned`, `blocked`, or `needs-repair`.\n4370-5. When all workers return, collect changed files, completed task ids, blockers, and assumptions.\n4371-6. Send the completed batch to `test-failure-attribution`.\n4372-7. When test failures return, dispatch fix workers for clear group-owned failures and dispatch `root-cause-analysis` for ambiguous failures.\n--\n4390-4. implementation-orchestrator\n4696:description: Orchestrate parallel implementation workers from complete independent task groups, collect their results, then coordinate test attribution, RCA, and repair loops. Use after task groups pass task-group-completeness and before any global test run.\n4697----\n4698-\n4699-# Implementation Orchestrator\n4700-\n4701-## A. Scope\n4702-\n4703:1. **Purpose:** Launch implementation workers from approved independent task groups and coordinate the batch until every group has returned a result.\n4704-2. **Ownership:** Own dispatch, worker result collection, test attribution handoff, root-cause routing, and repair-loop coordination.\n4705:3. **Boundary:** Do not implement code directly unless the orchestrator is explicitly assigned an `implementation-worker` role for one group.\n4706-\n4707----\n4708-\n4709-## B. Required Inputs\n4710-\n4711-1. **Task groups:** Read the approved independent groups from `task-group-completeness`.\n4712-2. **Dependency graph:** Read group ordering and blocking edges from `task-dependency`.\n4713-3. **Task inventory:** Read source task ids, target paths, acceptance checks, and evidence links from `task-list`.\n4714:4. **Worker contract:** Identify the implementation worker skill used for each dispatch.\n4715-5. **Test contract:** Identify the `test-failure-attribution` input format that receives the completed batch.\n4716-\n4717----\n4718-\n4719-## C. Dispatch Workflow\n4720-\n4721-1. **Build packages:** Create one dispatch package per ready group with `groupId`, `taskIds`, target paths, acceptance checks, source references, and forbidden out-of-scope areas.\n4722:2. **Launch workers:** Start one implementation worker for each independent group using available agent tooling.\n4723:3. **Protect global tests:** Do not run global tests while implementation workers are active.\n4724-4. **Track status:** Use the exact worker statuses `pending`, `running`, `returned`, `blocked`, and `needs-repair`.\n4725-5. **Collect returns:** When every worker has returned, collect changed files, completed task ids, blockers, and assumptions.\n4726-6. **Handoff tests:** Send the completed batch to `test-failure-attribution` with the test commands, changed files, completed task ids, and worker notes.\n4727-7. **Route failures:** Dispatch fix workers for clear group-owned failures and dispatch `root-cause-analysis` for ambiguous failures.\n--\n4747-4. **No requirement inference:** Do not ask a worker to infer missing requirements that should have been handled by `task-group-completeness`.\n4748-````\n4749-\n4750-# Dispatch Workflow\n5165-\n5166-1. **Build packages:** Create one dispatch package per ready group with `groupId`, `taskIds`, target paths, acceptance checks, source references, and forbidden out-of-scope areas.\n5167:2. **Launch workers:** Start one implementation worker for each independent group using available agent tooling.\n5168:3. **Protect global tests:** Do not run global tests while implementation workers are active.\n5169-4. **Track status:** Use the exact worker statuses `pending`, `running`, `returned`, `blocked`, and `needs-repair`.\n5170-5. **Collect returns:** When every worker has returned, collect changed files, completed task ids, blockers, and assumptions.\n5171-6. **Handoff tests:** Send the completed batch to `test-failure-attribution` with the test commands, changed files, completed task ids, and worker notes.\n5172-7. **Route failures:** Dispatch fix workers for clear group-owned failures and dispatch `root-cause-analysis` for ambiguous failures.\n--\n5192-4. **No requirement inference:** Do not ask a worker to infer missing requirements that should have been handled by `task-group-completeness`.\n5193-````\n5194-\n5195-# Use after task groups pass task-group-completeness and before any global test run.\n6075----\n6076-\n6077-# Implementation Orchestrator\n6078-\n6079-## A. Scope\n6080-\n6081:1. Launch implementation workers from **approved independent task groups** and coordinate the batch until every group has returned a result.\n6082-2. Own `dispatch`, `worker result collection`, `test attribution handoff`, `root-cause routing`, and `repair-loop coordination`.\n6083:3. Do not implement code directly unless the orchestrator is explicitly assigned an `implementation-worker` role for one group.\n6084-\n6085----\n6086-\n6087-## B. Required Inputs\n6088-\n6089-1. Read approved independent groups from `task-group-completeness`.\n6090-2. Read group ordering and blocking edges from `task-dependency`.\n6091-3. Read source `taskIds`, `targetPaths`, `acceptanceChecks`, and evidence links from `task-list`.\n6092:4. Identify the implementation worker skill used for each `dispatch`.\n6093-5. Identify the `test-failure-attribution` input format that receives the completed batch.\n6094-\n6095----\n6096-\n6097-## C. Dispatch Workflow\n6098-\n6099-1. Create one `dispatch package` per ready group with `groupId`, `taskIds`, `targetPaths`, `acceptanceChecks`, `sourceReferences`, and `forbiddenScopes`.\n6100:2. Start **one implementation worker per independent group** using available agent tooling.\n6101:3. Do not run `global tests` while implementation workers are active.\n6102-4. Track worker status with `pending`, `running`, `returned`, `blocked`, and `needs-repair`.\n6103-5. After every worker returns, collect `changedFiles`, `completedTaskIds`, `blockers`, and `assumptions`.\n6104-6. Send the completed batch to `test-failure-attribution` with `testCommands`, `changedFiles`, `completedTaskIds`, and worker notes.\n6105-7. Dispatch fix workers for **clear group-owned failures** and dispatch `root-cause-analysis` for ambiguous failures.\n--\n6125-4. Do not ask a worker to infer missing requirements that should have been handled by `task-group-completeness`.\n6126-````\n6127-\n6128-# AGENT\n6129:<!-- decision-os:note {\"id\":\"codex-codex-skill-1783596089570-85eceea5-line-111\",\"timestamp\":\"2026-07-09T15:43:28.067Z\",\"status\":\"in_progress\",\"codexRunId\":\"codex-skill-1783596089570-85eceea5\",\"codexLine\":\"111\",\"codexKind\":\"tool_call\",\"codexEventType\":\"item.started\",\"codexItemId\":\"item_29\",\"codexTool\":\"/usr/bin/zsh -lc \\\"rg -n '\\\\\\\\*\\\\\\\\*' .decision-os/cards/skills/card-skill-implementation-orchestrator.md\\\"\"} -->\n6130-\n6131:**Tool call** `/usr/bin/zsh -lc \"rg -n '\\\\*\\\\*' .decision-os/cards/skills/card-skill-implementation-orchestrator.md\"`\n6132-Status: in_progress\n6133-\n6134-# AGENT\n6135:<!-- decision-os:note {\"id\":\"codex-codex-skill-1783596089570-85eceea5-line-112\",\"timestamp\":\"2026-07-09T15:43:28.067Z\",\"status\":\"completed\",\"codexRunId\":\"codex-skill-1783596089570-85eceea5\",\"codexLine\":\"112\",\"codexKind\":\"tool_call\",\"codexEventType\":\"item.completed\",\"codexItemId\":\"item_29\",\"codexTool\":\"/usr/bin/zsh -lc \\\"rg -n '\\\\\\\\*\\\\\\\\*' .decision-os/cards/skills/card-skill-implementation-orchestrator.md\\\"\",\"codexExitCode\":\"0\"} -->\n6136-\n6137:**Tool call** `/usr/bin/zsh -lc \"rg -n '\\\\*\\\\*' .decision-os/cards/skills/card-skill-implementation-orchestrator.md\"`\n6138-Status: completed\n6139-Exit code: 0\n6140-\n6141-````text\n6142:10:1. Scope\\n+\\n+1. **Source material:** compared the two public prompt files referenced by the operator: `OpenAI/gpt-5.5-thinking.md` and `Anthropic/claude-fable-5.md` from `https://github.com/asgeirtj/system_prompts_leaks`.\\n+2. **Local analysis copy:** fetched both files into `/tmp/system_prompts_leaks` for complete structural review: `OpenAI/gpt-5.5-thinking.md` has `1,991` lines and `Anthropic/claude-fable-5.md` has `3,825` lines.\\n+3. **Authenticity limit:** treat both files as public repository artifacts, not independently verified vendor system prompts.\\n+4. **Copyright and confidentiality limit:** the full prompt text was used for analysis, but this card does not reproduce the complete source prompts verbatim.\\n+5. **Operator question:** identify the strengths of each system, especially what `Claude Fable 5` contains that is absent or weaker in `GPT-5.5 Thinking`, with emphasis on software engineering, planning, implementation, architecture, and design-system behavior.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## B. Executive Thesis\\n+\\n+1. **GPT-5.5 Thinking architecture:** the OpenAI prompt reads like a compact runtime contract for a general ChatGPT surface. It emphasizes tool schemas, web freshness, citations, multimodal handling, artifact handoff, scheduled automations, memory/user settings, and response style.\\n+2. **Claude Fable 5 architecture:** the Anthropic prompt reads like a larger assistant operating system. It defines product identity, safety subdomains, memory policy, persistent artifact storage, MCP app routing, past-chat retrieval, preference application, skills-first computer use, file lifecycle, visual routing, search strategy, and deferred tool loading.\\n+3. **Core difference:** `GPT-5.5 Thinking` is stronger as a lean execution surface with precise tool and citation mechanics; `Claude Fable 5` is stronger as a planned agent workflow framework with more explicit lifecycle rules.\\n+4. **Most important Fable advantage:** Fable has a deeper task-routing and implementation framework before execution: `skills -> file strategy -> artifact criteria -> MCP/internal tool priority -> visualizer routing -> search scaling -> output sharing`.\\n+5. **Most important GPT advantage:** GPT has a less bloated prompt, clearer web citation syntax, first-class utilities like `finance`, `sports`, `weather`, `time`, `automations`, and strong platform-specific UI widget guidance.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## C. Shared System Design Patterns\\n+\\n+1. **Tool-first runtime:** both prompts define concrete tool schemas and constrain when tools should be used.\\n+2. **Freshness gate:** both require web/search for current, unstable, or niche information rather than relying on static model knowledge.\\n+3. **Citation discipline:** both include citation/copyright constraints for sourced answers.\\n+4. **Artifact support:** both support generated files or UI artifacts, but with different routing models.\\n+5. **Personalization:** both include memory, preferences, or user-context application with limits.\\n+6. **Multimodal support:** both include image or visual-generation pathways, though Fable separates visual routing more explicitly.\\n+7. **Style control:** both prompts include tone, verbosity, and response-format instructions.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## D. GPT-5.5 Strengths Not Fully Matched By Fable\\n+\\n+1. **Compact prompt surface:** GPT carries fewer top-level behavioral modules. This reduces instruction collision risk and leaves more context for the user task.\\n+2. **Precise citation grammar:** GPT specifies exact web citation syntax, source reference handling, placement rules, and line/file citation expectations for uploaded or searched documents.\\n+3. **First-class utility APIs:** GPT exposes structured commands for `finance`, `sports`, `weather`, `time`, `calculator`, product search, image search, and web search in one unified `web.run` style.\\n+4. **Scheduled work model:** GPT has an explicit `automations` namespace for future or recurring tasks, including schedule constraints and failure handling. Fable's prompt does not expose an equivalent automation subsystem in the inspected file.\\n+5. **Canvas and document iteration:** GPT includes `canmore` behavior for long-lived editable canvases and code/document textdocs. Fable uses file/artifact creation, but the OpenAI canvas model is more directly oriented toward iterative in-chat documents.\\n+6. **User settings controls:** GPT exposes user-facing controls such as `user_settings`, `bio`, `personal_context`, and memory update flows in the runtime tool stack.\\n+7. **Direct platform widgets:** GPT's rich UI sections define when to show image carousels, product carousels, navigation lists, weather widgets, sports widgets, stock charts, and math widgets.\\n+8. **Lower procedural overhead:** GPT has fewer mandatory preflight steps. For simple tasks, this can produce faster answers and fewer self-imposed detours.\\n+9. **Better directness rules:** GPT has strong style constraints such as avoiding meta-commentary, avoiding specific filler phrases, and keeping responses readable without overusing lists.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## E. Claude Fable 5 Strengths Not Fully Matched By GPT-5.5\\n+\\n+1. **Agent operating system structure:** Fable uses explicit XML-like modules such as `claude_behavior`, `memory_system`, `computer_use`, `request_evaluation_checklist`, `search_instructions`, and tool sections. This makes the prompt more modular and easier to reason about as a product architecture.\\n+2. **Product ecosystem routing:** Fable knows how to position `Claude Code`, `Claude Cowork`, `Claude in Chrome`, `Claude in Excel`, and `Claude in PowerPoint`, and can recommend apps when a task fits a specialized product surface.\\n+3. **Skills-first implementation discipline:** before creating files, writing code, or running computer tools, Fable requires reading relevant `SKILL.md` files. This is a strong engineering control because it turns hidden environment knowledge into an explicit preflight step.\\n+4. **File lifecycle contract:** Fable specifies when to create files, where uploads live, where scratch work belongs, where final outputs belong, when to use `present_files`, and how to choose between inline answers and durable artifacts.\\n+5. **Artifact architecture:** Fable defines artifact criteria, supported artifact types, single-file expectations for HTML/React, package rules, and restrictions such as avoiding unsupported browser storage APIs.\\n+6. **Persistent artifact storage:** Fable includes a `window.storage` API with key design, shared/private scope, failure handling, and progressive loading guidance. GPT's inspected prompt does not provide an equivalent persistent artifact storage design.\\n+7. **Visual routing DAG:** Fable has a request-evaluation checklist: decide whether a visual is needed, prefer a connected MCP tool when it fits, use file tools when a file is requested, otherwise use the Visualizer. This is closer to product-grade UX routing than GPT's image/widget guidance.\\n+8. **Design-system-aware visualizer:** Fable requires loading visualizer modules such as `diagram`, `mockup`, `interactive`, `data_viz`, `art`, and `chart`, and treats CSS variables, dimensions, typography, and layout rules as authoritative design context.\\n+9. **MCP connector governance:** Fable has a detailed registry and opt-in policy for third-party MCP apps, including when to search for connectors, when to suggest them, when to call them directly, and when to fall back to browser/search.\\n+10. **Past-chat retrieval heuristics:** Fable provides detailed linguistic cues for when to search prior conversations, how to form compact search queries, and how to synthesize snippets without exposing irrelevant personal details.\\n+11. **Memory application policy:** Fable has a full memory subsystem: when to apply memory, when not to, forbidden phrases, examples, direct factual question handling, emotional boundaries, and a separate memory-edit tool guide.\\n+12. **Wellbeing and interpersonal boundaries:** Fable has more detailed user-wellbeing, criticism, abuse, mental-health, and self-destructive-behavior handling than GPT's inspected prompt.\\n+13. **Safety granularity:** Fable contains highly granular child-safety, weapons, harmful substances, malicious-code, legal/financial, political evenhandedness, copyright, and harmful-search constraints.\\n+14. **Search scaling model:** Fable distinguishes one-search facts, medium research, deep research, internal-tool precedence, search query construction, source fetching, and when to suggest a research feature.\\n+15. **Implementation planning primitives:** Fable gives concrete triggers such as when `>10` lines of code should become a file, when long content should be built iteratively, and when to verify tool availability.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## F. Software Engineering Implications\\n+\\n+1. **Preflight quality:** Fable is stronger for implementation tasks that require environment-specific constraints because the prompt makes skill discovery mandatory before code/file work.\\n+2. **Artifact reliability:** Fable is stronger for generated deliverables because it defines scratch paths, output paths, sharing behavior, artifact type selection, persistence, and rendering constraints.\\n+3. **Architecture diagrams and product UX:** Fable is stronger for visual architecture work because it has an explicit visual-routing DAG and design-system module loading before rendering.\\n+4. **Connector-based workflows:** Fable is stronger for productized agent workflows that touch calendars, email, tasks, issue trackers, apps, or partner services because it specifies connector discovery and consent.\\n+5. **Long-horizon personalization:** Fable is stronger for continuity across conversations because it separates memory, past-chat search, preferences, and contextual application.\\n+6. **Simple execution speed:** GPT is stronger for low-complexity tasks because it avoids mandatory broad preflight checks and has a smaller instruction stack.\\n+7. **Web-grounded answers:** GPT is stronger when exact citation mechanics, source references, and UI result widgets matter more than agentic workflow planning.\\n+8. **Scheduled operations:** GPT is stronger for reminders and recurring tasks because `automations` is a first-class runtime subsystem.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## G. Planning And Implementation Comparison\\n+\\n+1. **GPT planning model:** GPT relies on concise tool rules and general honesty/factuality constraints. It plans implicitly unless a task requires tools, citations, artifacts, or automation.\\n+2. **Fable planning model:** Fable defines explicit routing layers before execution: skill selection, file-vs-inline decision, MCP-vs-visualizer decision, search depth, internal-vs-web source priority, and output sharing.\\n+3. **GPT implementation model:** GPT is optimized for direct tool invocation with strong schemas. It is efficient when the correct tool is obvious.\\n+4. **Fable implementation model:** Fable is optimized for repeatable delivery workflows. It gives the assistant a process for producing files, code, artifacts, visuals, and connector-backed actions with fewer missing lifecycle steps.\\n+5. **GPT verification model:** GPT emphasizes source trust, citations, and honesty about failed work.\\n+6. **Fable verification model:** Fable adds implementation-specific verification: check tool availability, handle storage errors, show loading states, and present final files through the correct output channel.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## H. Architecture And Design-System Comparison\\n+\\n+1. **GPT architecture style:** schema-first, tool-list-heavy, platform-feature-oriented, and compact.\\n+2. **Fable architecture style:** module-first, lifecycle-heavy, product-surface-aware, and procedural.\\n+3. **GPT design-system posture:** supports generated images and rich UI widgets, but mostly through individual feature instructions.\\n+4. **Fable design-system posture:** treats visuals as a routed product surface with module-specific constraints, CSS variables, layout rules, platform targeting, and proactive visualization triggers.\\n+5. **GPT artifact posture:** supports documents, spreadsheets, slides, canvas, and generated artifacts, but the inspected prompt does not define a full artifact storage API.\\n+6. **Fable artifact posture:** treats artifacts as software products with persistence, storage keys, loading/error states, package constraints, and output delivery.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## I. Fable 5 Additions Over GPT-5.5\\n+\\n+1. **More complete agent workflow stack:** Fable adds a clear chain from task classification to tool selection to file/artifact output.\\n+2. **More implementation guardrails:** Fable adds mandatory skills, package-management notes, file-location rules, output-sharing rules, and artifact criteria.\\n+3. **More product-surface intelligence:** Fable adds app recommendation and product routing across chat, code, coworking, browser, spreadsheet, and slides surfaces.\\n+4. **More memory governance:** Fable adds detailed rules for applying memory, searching past chats, avoiding meta-memory language, and handling memory edits.\\n+5. **More visual product design:** Fable adds visualizer routing, module loading, proactive visualization, multi-visual sequencing, and design constraints.\\n+6. **More connector policy:** Fable adds registry search, connector suggestion, third-party opt-in, and internal-tool priority.\\n+7. **More persistent app architecture:** Fable adds `window.storage` for artifacts, including key design, shared scope, and failure handling.\\n+8. **More safety specificity:** Fable has more granular domain-specific safety sections and refusal rules.\\n+9. **More explicit research scaling:** Fable tells the model how many searches/tools to use for simple, medium, deep, and excessive research tasks.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## J. Risks And Tradeoffs\\n+\\n+1. **Fable prompt bloat risk:** the prompt is nearly twice as long as the GPT file. More instructions can mean more context pressure, more conflicts, and slower task startup.\\n+2. **Fable over-process risk:** mandatory skill reads before code/files/bash can improve quality, but may be excessive for trivial commands or quick diagnostics.\\n+3. **Fable product-marketing risk:** embedding product family claims and app recommendations in the core prompt can age quickly and may create stale behavior.\\n+4. **Fable conflict risk:** artifact storage guidance and browser-storage restrictions can conflict depending on the execution surface.\\n+5. **GPT under-specification risk:** GPT's compact prompt leaves more lifecycle decisions implicit, which can cause weaker file routing, less systematic design output, or missed preflight steps.\\n+6. **GPT product workflow gap:** GPT has many tools, but less explicit governance for connector selection, app routing, and user consent around third-party services.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## K. Recommendations For Decision-OS Prompt Engineering\\n+\\n+1. **Borrow Fable's lifecycle DAG:** add explicit routing for `inline answer -> card update -> repo edit -> generated artifact -> visual mockup -> server action`.\\n+2. **Borrow Fable's skills preflight selectively:** require skill reads for file/code/artifact/UI work, but avoid making every shell command pay that cost.\\n+3. **Borrow Fable's artifact contract:** define scratch paths, final paths, render/verify steps, storage constraints, and sharing rules for decision-os outputs.\\n+4. **Borrow Fable's visual routing:** before making mockups or diagrams, decide whether the deliverable is a card prose update, standalone image, HTML/CSS mockup, Mermaid/SVG diagram, or repo UI change.\\n+5. **Borrow Fable's connector consent model:** if decision-os later integrates external tools, define `discover -> suggest -> explicit operator choice -> execute` for third-party actions.\\n+6. **Keep GPT's compactness:** do not copy Fable's full breadth. Convert useful Fable behavior into small, decision-os-specific contracts.\\n+7. **Keep GPT's citation rigor:** maintain exact source handling, line references, and explicit uncertainty when source authenticity is not verified.\\n+8. **Avoid anti-specs:** every prompt rule added to decision-os should introduce a concrete requirement, constraint, decision, evidence rule, or action.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## L. Direct Answer\\n+\\n+1. **What Fable 5 has that GPT-5.5 does not:** Fable has a more complete agent engineering framework: `skills`, `file_creation_advice`, `artifact_usage_criteria`, `persistent_storage_for_artifacts`, `mcp_app_suggestions`, `past_chats_tools`, `memory_application_examples`, `request_evaluation_checklist`, `visualizer` modules, and detailed search-scaling rules.\\n+2. **What GPT-5.5 has that Fable 5 does not emphasize as strongly:** GPT has a cleaner tool/citation runtime, first-class automation, richer utility widgets, and less prompt overhead.\\n+3. **Best software-engineering interpretation:** GPT is a strong general execution interface; Fable is a stronger planning-and-delivery scaffold for complex agentic work.\\n+4. **Best architectural takeaway:** use Fable's lifecycle and routing concepts, but compress them into decision-os-specific rules so the system gains implementation rigor without inheriting the full prompt operator choosing which planning or execution skill to use for a broad goal, weak ticket, product decomposition, feature plan, bug plan, or executor-led implementation scaffold.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## 1. What is this for?\\n+\\n+1. **This inventory prevents using one planning skill for every job.** The source separates goal normalization, ticket improvement, product decomposition, feature planning, bug RCA, OpenSpec task creation, executor scaffolding, and downstream implementation.\\n+2. **The key correction is that earlier findings must be merged, not replaced.** `ticket-solver`, `openticket`, `improveticket`, `product-analysis`, and the executor skills remain part of the planning inventory.\\n+3. **The operator choice depends on the desired workflow state.** Use local Codex skills for operator-facing issue preparation, OpenSpec skills for artifact-driven task lists, DroidFactory roles for GitLab pipeline progression, and executor skills for local implementation ledgers.\\n+4. **`ticket-solver` is not the broad-goal starting point.** It belongs after a ticket exists and can then create a working DAG, implement, test, and report evidence.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## 2. Which entry point should the operator choose?\\n+\\n+1. **Broad operator problem to approved GitLab issue:** use `openticket`. It performs code-first analysis, drafts requirements, scope, impact, blockers, DAG, and acceptance checks, then opens the issue after approval.\\n+2. **Existing weak issue:** use `improveticket` locally, or `ticket/improver` in DroidFactory. Both normalize the issue; the Factory role also classifies it into `feature` or `bug` pipeline flow.\\n+3. **OpenSpec goal to task list:** use `openspec-ff-change`. It creates the OpenSpec artifact sequence through `tasks.md`, which is the implementation checklist.\\n+4. **Product goal that must become many tickets:** use the DroidFactory product and epic chain, ending in feature issues that can enter feature planning.\\n+5. **Single feature or bug already scoped:** use `feature/analyzer -> feature/planner` for feature work, and `bug/rca` for bug work.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## 3. How are the planning systems shaped?\\n+\\n+1. **Local Codex planning prepares or upgrades work.** `openticket`, `improveticket`, and `product-analysis` help define the problem or issue before downstream execution.\\n+2. **OpenSpec planning creates ordered artifacts.** The planning path runs from proposal to spec to design to `tasks.md`; `openspec-apply-change` executes only after that structure exists.\\n+3. **DroidFactory planning is label-driven.** Product, epic, feature, bug, research, and refactor pipelines progress through labeled stages and role-specific outputs.\\n+4. **Executor planning is ledger-driven.** `executor-precheck`, `executor-stack`, and `executor-spec` build toward a `Master Ledger`; `executor-implement` consumes that ledger rather than inventing architecture.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## 4. What are the main handoffs?\\n+\\n+1. **Factory broad-goal chain:** `ticket/improver -> product/analyzer/RFC/architecture/PRD -> product/decomposer -> epic/analyzer/architect/quality-planner -> epic/decomposer -> feature/analyzer -> feature/planner -> feature/implementer`.\\n+2. **Product decomposition handoff:** `product/decomposer` creates child epics; `epic/decomposer` creates child feature tickets.\\n+3. **Feature planning handoff:** `feature/analyzer` maps intent to code evidence, then `feature/planner` produces the implementation plan and `Ideal Control-flow DAG`.\\n+4. **Bug planning handoff:** `bug/rca` produces reproduction status, trace, root cause, fix scope, fix DAG, regression test plan, and fixer checklist before implementation.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## 5. What constraints affect use?\\n+\\n+1. **Do not treat analysis-only skills as implementers.** `product-analysis`, `openspec-explore`, research stages, and analyzer roles build evidence or plans but do not execute.\\n+2. **Do not ask implementation skills to infer missing planning structure.** `executor-implement`, `openspec-apply-change`, and `ticket-solver` should consume prepared plans, tickets, artifacts, or ledgers.\\n+3. **Use Factory when GitLab issues and labels are the workflow state.** Use executor skills when the desired output is a local `Master Ledger` implementation scaffold.\\n+4. **For bugs, start with RCA rather than feature planning.** The source identifies `bug/rca` as the bug planner because it produces the fix DAG and regression test plan.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## 6.
